Metamaterials are artificial electromagnetic materials engineered to exhibit properties not found in natural substances.
The term 'metamaterial' lacks a universally accepted definition but generally involves emergent properties beyond constituent materials.
Metamaterials often consist of periodic structures with lattice constants much smaller than the wavelength of interest.
Artificial dielectrics were among the earliest metamaterials, created by embedding metal spheres in a dielectric matrix.
Artificial magnetics generate magnetic response at microwave frequencies using resonant structures like split-ring resonators.
Chiral metamaterials exhibit optical rotatory power due to handed microstructures causing magnetoelectric coupling.
Veselago media have simultaneously negative permittivity and permeability, leading to negative refractive index phenomena.
Extreme-parameter media include materials with very large or very small permittivity and permeability values.
Bianisotropic media require a 36-parameter matrix to describe their electromagnetic constitutive relations.
The Perfect Electromagnetic Conductor (PEMC) is a theoretical metamaterial generalizing PEC and PMC boundary conditions.
Metamaterials can be designed to have emergent properties such as negative refraction, reversed Doppler shift, and inverse Cherenkov radiation.
The homogenization approach allows metamaterials to be treated as effective continuous media despite their discrete microstructure.
Not all engineered composites are metamaterials; the key is the emergence of new electromagnetic properties.
Periodic ordering in metamaterials facilitates predictable effective medium behavior but is not strictly necessary.
Metamaterials research has accelerated since the early 2000s with significant interdisciplinary interest.
Metamaterials enable applications in optics and microwaves including superlenses and antenna radomes.

The classification of metamaterials includes artificial dielectrics, artificial magnetics, chiral materials, Veselago media, extreme-parameter media, PEMC media, waveguiding media, and electromagnetic crystals.
Chiral media require uniform handedness of their microstructure to exhibit macroscopic optical activity.
The term 'meta' means 'beyond' or 'higher kind' and reflects the emergent nature of metamaterial properties.
Metamaterials can be sensitive to the size and arrangement of their microstructural scatterers, affecting their macroscopic response.
